body.heading: A tilted world
paragraphs: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees relative to its orbit. As we circle the Sun over a year, that tilt points first one hemisphere and then the other more directly toward the Sun. The hemisphere leaning in receives sunlight more directly and for longer days — its summer. The one leaning away gets slanted, weaker light and long nights — its winter.

The distance theory fails a simple test: Earth is actually near its closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter. If distance ruled the seasons, both hemispheres would share the same summer at once. Instead, when it is summer in Australia, it is winter in Europe — exactly what tilt predicts.

body.heading: Why the tilt changes everything
paragraphs: Two effects multiply. Direct light concentrates energy on a smaller patch of ground, heating it more. And longer days give that heating more hours to work. Together they easily outweigh the small change in our distance from the Sun across the year.

Planets with different tilts get different seasons: Uranus, tipped nearly on its side, has extreme seasons decades long, while Jupiter, barely tilted, has almost none. Our seasons are a consequence of a lean acquired in Earth's early history — possibly from the same collision that formed the Moon.

takeaway: Seasons come from Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt, which takes turns aiming each hemisphere at the Sun.
